_comment: The hand-authored core of the tap-a-word dictionary: the words that carry running
German and that neither the shared noun collection nor the verb collection knows.
Authored by hand on purpose. These are exactly the words a machine glosses badly:
'sich' is not 'himself', 'doch' is not a word English has, and 'der' is four
different cases wearing one spelling. A gloss here is allowed to teach — '(feminine
/ plural)' after an article, '(+ dative)' after a preposition — because the panel
shows it to a learner, not to a translation engine.
`forms` lists the other spellings that should resolve to this entry: inflections,
and the capitalised spelling only where a word is not already capitalised by the
sentence-start fallback. Run `node tool/build-dictionary.mjs --report` to see what
the content still uses that nothing here can gloss, most-used first.

entries.en: the (masculine; also feminine dative and genitive)
you (several people, informal) — or her / their
you, to you (plural informal) — or yourselves
himself, herself, itself, themselves — the reflexive that belongs to a verb
myself, yourself, itself — in person; also: even
at, on, to (+ dative or accusative)
at, near, at the home of (+ dative)
over, above, about (+ dative or accusative)
in front of, before, ago (+ dative or accusative)
next to, beside (+ dative or accusative)
since, for (a length of time) (+ dative)
because, for — keeps normal word order
that — sends the verb to the end
because — sends the verb to the end
when (one time in the past) — or: than, as
so that — or: with it, with that
so that, with the result that
all the more (second half of 'je ... umso')
that is why — or: around it
with it, at the same time
yes it is (contradicting a negative) — or a softener: 'do come in, won't you'
please — or: here you are / you're welcome
a softener in requests — or: times, once
already — or a softener: 'it'll be fine'
in a moment — or: the same
on the way, out and about
gladly — 'ich esse gern' means 'I like eating'
going on, loose — 'was ist los?' is 'what's up?'
the end of the working day
desire — 'Lust haben' is 'to feel like it'
to report, to get in touch
to observe, to pay attention to
to say goodbye — also: to pass a law
to seem — also: to take effect
to act — 'es handelt sich um' is 'it is about'
to deal with, to get done
to hold on to, to record
to read, to go (of a text)
to go into, to come in
to arrive — 'es kommt darauf an' is 'it depends'
to get to know, to meet
to turn — 'sich wenden an' is 'to turn to'
could, is said to be able to (reported speech)
Anytown — the placeholder city on German forms
greeting — 'Mit freundlichen Grüßen' ends a formal letter
nominative — the case of the subject
accusative — the case of the direct object
dative — the case of the indirect object
genitive — the case that shows possession
